lesson_title: One Rand, Many Pockets: the Multiplier
hook_text: A municipality pays a pipe crew R2 000. The town ends up R8 000 richer. Watch.
clip_script: A Limpopo municipality replaces the burst pipe on main street and pays a local crew two thousand rand. Follow the money. The fitter banks five hundred for his son's college fund and spends fifteen hundred — chicken at the butchery, electricity units, a taxi to town. That fifteen hundred is now the butchery's income. The butcher holds back a quarter and spends eleven twenty-five — flour from the bakery, a mended apron from the seamstress. The baker holds a quarter and spends about eight forty-four. Count the pockets one payment has filled: fitter, butcher, baker, seamstress, taxi owner, tuckshop. Add every round and the town's income rises by eight thousand rand — four times the original job. That is the multiplier. Now the catch. At every pocket a slice steps out: some SAVED, some TAXED, some spent on IMPORTS — and the import slice leaves South Africa forever. If half of every rand exits each round, your two thousand adds four thousand, not eight. Same pipe, same crew, half the effect. Which is why WHO receives the money and WHAT it buys decide how far one rand can travel.
visual_style: A single banknote hopping between shopfronts on a small-town main street, a slice peeling off at each stop into a bank book, a till receipt and a departing container, the remainder shrinking but hopping on.
pacing: Quick hand-offs through the six pockets, a hard stop at the leak, steady close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run any multiplier — forwards or backwards — in one line.
